analogy.title: GPS Navigation, Not a Printed Map
analogy.text: A printed map gives you the route once and hopes you don't miss a turn. A GPS recalculates in real time based on where you actually are. The ODF works exactly like that — it loops, adapts, and always recalculates based on real delivery progress, not where a plan said you'd be.

list.name: 01 — Intent & Outcome Definition
list.desc: Define the business goal in one clear sentence. Identify stakeholders, success metrics, and the specific problem being solved. Precision here prevents all downstream drift.

list.name: 02 — Requirements & Context
list.desc: Capture all business needs, constraints, technical context, and boundaries. AI cannot design well without full context — this stage makes that context explicit and complete.

list.name: 03 — AI-Assisted Design
list.desc: AI generates the architecture, solution designs, data models, and API contracts. The Lead reviews and approves. AI doesn't just code — it designs the blueprint first.

list.name: 04 — AI-Generated Development
list.desc: AI accelerates the actual coding — frontend, backend, APIs, integrations. One focused prompt per component, validated before the next one begins.

list.name: 05 — Testing & Quality Assurance
list.desc: AI-assisted and human-led validation. Every acceptance criterion tested. Security, data isolation, edge cases, and error handling — all verified systematically. Not a vibe check — a gate.

list.name: 06 — Deployment & Improvement
list.desc: Deliver rapidly and continuously evolve. Deploy to staging then production. Every release is documented, tested, and reversible. Stakeholder feedback triggers the next improvement loop.

slides.title: The Five Ways Intent Goes Wrong
slides.subtitle: Avoid these — they're the most common mistakes in the field

analogy.title: The 'Close Enough' Trap
analogy.text: 'Close enough' is the most expensive phrase in software. A vague intent that seems 80% right generates code that's 80% right — and that last 20% costs more to fix than writing the whole intent properly would have.

list.name: The Vague Outcome
list.desc: 'Build a dashboard for managers.' No scope, no role def, no data spec. Fix: specify exact role, exact metrics, exact data sources, exact acceptance criteria.

list.name: The Mega-Prompt
list.desc: One prompt for the entire app. Quality degrades with scope. Fix: one focused prompt per component, validate each before next.

list.name: The Assumption Prompt
list.desc: 'Add authentication.' No stack, no existing patterns, no token strategy. Fix: specify exact mechanism, reference existing code.

list.name: The Trust-and-Skip
list.desc: Accepting output without checking. AI is statistically good but not always correct. Fix: validate every output. No exceptions.

list.name: The Manual Patch
list.desc: Fixing code by hand instead of re-prompting. Creates drift between intent and implementation. Fix: always correct through prompting.

slides.subtitle: Not a vibe check — a systematic gate

analogy.title: Restaurant Health Inspection
analogy.text: A health inspector doesn't walk in and go 'yeah, feels clean.' They have a checklist. Every item checked. Every item documented. Your validation is the same — systematic, documented, no shortcuts.

list.name: Functional Correctness
list.desc: Does every acceptance criterion produce the correct behaviour? Test each one explicitly.

list.name: Business Rule Enforcement
list.desc: Is every validation rule enforced server-side, not only in the UI? Can it be bypassed via API?

list.name: Data Isolation
list.desc: Can User A see User B's data in any code path? Test cross-tenant access explicitly.

list.name: Error Handling
list.desc: Does every error return a clear, user-appropriate message? No stack traces, no internal paths.

list.name: Security
list.desc: Auth guards on every endpoint. Authorization at service layer. Parameterized queries. No PII in responses.

list.name: Edge Cases
list.desc: Empty inputs, boundary values, concurrent requests — all the edge cases from the intent.

list.name: Documentation
list.desc: Has auto-generated documentation accurately captured what was built, including decisions?

analogy.title: The Cooking Show Format
analogy.text: Cooking shows don't show you the recipe and say 'figure it out.' They show you the chef doing it — step by step, with commentary. That's what this slide is. One feature, full lifecycle, play by play.

timeline.desc: Stakeholder says: 'We need employees to submit expenses.' You define the outcome in one sentence, identify 3 stakeholder roles, and list success metrics and acceptance criteria before AI touches anything.
Document all business needs: 6 validation rules, expense categories, approval workflow, tech stack constraints. Full context captured so AI can design accurately.
AI generates: ExpenseReport data model, API contracts for 4 endpoints, component architecture blueprint. Lead reviews and approves the design before development begins.
Prompt 1: DB migrations. Prompt 2: service layer with business rules. Prompt 3: API endpoints with guards. Prompt 4: React form with validation. Each validated before next.
All 6 validation rules tested. Server-side enforcement confirmed. Manager can't see other teams' expenses. Error messages clean. Edge cases covered. Gate passed.
Deployed to staging. Demo at 2PM — stakeholder requests receipt upload. New requirement captured, loop restarts at Stage 01. Feature live by 4:30 with improvement queued.

scenario.label: The Scenario
scenario.text: A client says: 'We need a leave request system. Employees request leave, managers approve or reject, and HR can see all requests.' That's the entire brief. slides.task_prompt: Write the 8-component intent statement and orchestrate the build plan. Fill in the fields below.

input_fields.label: Outcome
input_fields.placeholder: One sentence: what working behaviour should exist?

input_fields.label: Actor & Role
input_fields.placeholder: List all user roles and their permissions

input_fields.label: Validation Rules (numbered)
input_fields.placeholder: What makes input valid or invalid?

input_fields.label: Build Order (numbered)
input_fields.placeholder: What gets generated first, second, third...?

input_fields.label: Key API Endpoints

model_answer.outcome: Build a leave request system where Employees submit requests, Managers approve/reject team requests, and HR views all requests.
model_answer.actor_role: EMPLOYEE (request leave, view own history), MANAGER (view/approve/reject team leave), HR (view all leave requests, no edit).
model_answer.validation_rules: (1) leave dates must be in future, (2) start date <= end date, (3) description mandatory, (4) leave duration cannot exceed remaining balance.
model_answer.security: JWT auth. Managers can only access requests where submitter's managerId matches Manager's ID. HR role required for global read endpoint.
model_answer.build_order: (1) Prisma schema with LeaveRequest model and migrations, (2) NestJS Service layer with validation rules, (3) Controller endpoints with Guards, (4) React forms and tables.
model_answer.api_contracts: POST /leave (Employee, submit), GET /leave/team (Manager, view team), PATCH /leave/:id/approve (Manager, action), GET /leave/all (HR, view all).

comparison_report.title: How did your plan stack up?
comparison_report.intro: This lab tests your ability to structure intent and define a clean build sequence before prompting. Let's compare your plan to the model answer.

common_gaps.insight: Did you catch that Managers must be restricted to their own team? Client-side hidden lists aren't enough — it must be enforced server-side via SQL/ORM conditions.
Database migrations must come first. Generating controllers before the schema results in import errors and compiler noise.

comparison_report.closing_line: Review the differences and proceed to Lab 2 when you're ready.

slides.subtitle: Can you turn acceptance criteria into explicit test actions?

scenario.label: The Scenario
scenario.text: Using the leave request feature from Lab 1, your AI just generated the service layer and API endpoints. Before you accept this code, you need a validation checklist. For each acceptance criterion below, write the specific test action you'd perform.

slides.task_prompt: Define specific test actions for validation. Fill in the fields below.

input_fields.label: Functional Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify an employee can submit a leave request?

input_fields.label: Business Rule Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify overlapping leave dates are rejected?

input_fields.label: Data Isolation Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify Employee A can't see Employee B's requests?

input_fields.label: Security Test
input_fields.placeholder: How do you verify the API rejects unauthenticated requests?

input_fields.label: Edge Case Test
input_fields.placeholder: What happens when an employee requests leave for a past date?

input_fields.label: Error Handling Test
input_fields.placeholder: What does the user see when submitting an invalid request?

model_answer.functional: Use Swagger/Postman to POST a valid leave request payload as Employee A. Verify 201 Created response and DB record existence.
model_answer.business_rule: Submit a leave request for July 1-5, then submit another for July 3-7 for same Employee. Verify 400 Bad Request on second.
model_answer.data_isolation: Log in as Manager A. Attempt GET /leave/team. Verify only requests from Employee A (team member) are returned, no Employee B (Manager B's team) requests.
model_answer.security: Make GET /leave/all request without Authorization header. Verify 401 Unauthorized response is returned.
model_answer.edge_case: Submit leave request with startDate in past (e.g. yesterday). Verify API validation rejects it with clear validation error.
model_answer.error_handling: Submit a request missing dates. Verify response contains detailed JSON error list showing validation errors, not a 500 error.

comparison_report.title: Checklist Validation
comparison_report.intro: A true OrchestrAI Lead tests systematically. Let's compare your validation test actions with the model answers.

common_gaps.insight: Always test with cross-tenant context. Trying to fetch data using another user's ID is the absolute best way to check if your server-side checks actually hold up.
Ensure bad payloads return 400 with messages. If you get a 500 response, that's a validation leak — the database crashed instead of the API catching it.
